jobs.text: Prologue
Torben Mehring
Hamburg-Blankenese, Elbe beach, 4 November 2024, 7:15 a.m.
In November, the Elbe gives nothing up willingly.
What it does spit out, it has kept long enough.
I'm standing on the gravel below the Falkensteiner bank, hands in my pockets, and the drizzle is finding its way into my collar.
Crime scene investigation has set up two floodlights.
Their light turns the grey dawn into something clinical that doesn't belong here.
A man with a Labrador found her, just after six.
He's sitting in the ambulance, a blanket around his shoulders, gripping the lead as if the dog might be taken from him too.
Petra Brenner comes up the bank, the hood of her overall pulled low over her face.
Twenty years in crime scene investigation.
She's developed a voice that loses all colour when things are bad.
Today she has that voice.
"Female, young. Seventeen, eighteen maybe. Asian origin, as far as one can still tell."
She pulls off her gloves.
"She was weighed down. The rope has chafed through, cheap synthetic fiber. I'd say two months in the water, probably a bit more."
"Cause of death?"
"Strangulation marks on the neck, hyoid bone likely fractured. And there are indications of sexual violence. Forensic medicine will give you more detail."
I write it down.
My notebook is leather, old, the corners worn soft from handling.
Colleagues type their notes into tablets.
I need the scratch of the pen to think.
"ID?"
"Nothing. But this."
Brenner hands me an evidence bag.
Inside, a fine gold chain with an oval pendant.
Someone has engraved three letters into the gold, in an ornate script that looks like a jeweler on Neuer Wall.
K. v. T.
I turn the bag in the light.
No girl who ends up in the Elbe wears a chain like that.
And no girl who wears a chain like that disappears for two months without all of Hamburg looking for her.
In thirty years I've learned to pay attention to contradictions like that.
Most of the time they're just coincidence.
Not this time.
Chapter 1
Cindy Bergmann
Hamburg, university, 15 July 2024, 10:30 a.m.
I'm sitting in the back row.
People who sit at the back get looked at less often.
I learned that in eleven years of foster families, long before I knew what a strategy was.
The seminar room smells of new carpet and cleaning products.
Summer light falls through the wall of windows, and outside on the lawn students are lying around as if they'd never done anything else.
Twenty applicants from all over northern Germany are sitting here, competing for a single full scholarship from the Lindqvist Foundation.
Four years at MIT.
Tuition, flights, housing, everything.
I'm the only one wearing a sweater from Oxfam.
Three euros, dark blue, a small hole in the left sleeve.
I keep my arms crossed so no one sees it.
Werner doesn't know I'm here.
For three months I wrote the application at night, after he'd fallen asleep in front of the television.
Printed it in the school library, twenty cents a page, paid for with deposit bottles.
Frau Sommer, my maths teacher, wrote the reference.
I told her my family was behind me.
Family.
I slide my hands under the table.
The skin on my fingers is cracked from washing up without gloves.
"Number seventeen, please."
The foundation uses numbers instead of names so that background doesn't matter.
As if you can't see it anyway.
I stand up.
And on the way to the front I see her.
Second row, on the aisle.
A girl with my face.
I stop.
The same black hair, only hers shines and falls in a cut that cost money.
The same eyes, only without the shadows beneath them.
The same slight crookedness to the nose that I always notice first in the mirror.
She is wearing a cream-colored blazer and a pearl necklace, and her hands rest calmly on a silver laptop.
She turns her head.
Our eyes meet.
Her mouth opens, very slightly.
"Number seventeen?"
The professor sounds impatient.
I keep walking.
My sneakers squeak on the floor, far too loud.
At the lectern, the projector throws my first slide onto the wall: Complexity Theory: Why Some Problems Remain Hard.
I know every sentence.
I have whispered it a hundred times, in my little room, so Werner won't hear me.
Now my head is empty.
I stammer.
I lose the thread at P versus NP, of all places.
The professor interrupts me twice.
Someone in the third row giggles.
And again and again my gaze drifts to the second row, to the face that looks at me as if I were the ghost.
After ten minutes the professor raises his hand.
"Thank you. That will do."
I walk back to my seat and stare at the desk.
My only way out of Steilshoop.
Burned in ten minutes.
When it's over, I'm the first one at the door.
I take the stairs instead of the lift, two steps at a time.
"Wait!"
A hand on my arm.
I spin around.
Up close it's worse.
Like a mirror hanging in another life.
She smells of a perfume I don't know.
I smell of discount-store shower gel.
"We need to talk," she says.
"This can't be a coincidence."
"I have to go."
My standard line.
It has saved me many times before.
"Please. One hour."
Her grip is gentle, but she doesn't let go.
"My name is Katharina. Katharina von Tiefenbach."
Of course that's her name.
"Cindy," I say.
"Bergmann."
She repeats my name quietly, as if she has to learn it first.
"Cindy. Do you know what we are?"
I do know.
I knew it the moment she turned her head.
I should leave.
Instead I nod.
For the first time in my life, I want something more than to get away.
Chapter 2
Katharina von Tiefenbach
Hamburg-Rotherbaum, Café Schöne Aussichten, 15 July 2024, 12:00 p.m.
I order two chai lattes before she can say anything.
Five euros twenty a glass.
I see her gaze catch briefly on the price board, and I feel ashamed without knowing exactly what for.
We sit in a corner with a view of the Alster.
She sits on the edge of her chair, her bag in her lap.
As if she wanted to be able to leave at any moment.
"I'm adopted," I say.
There is no elegant way to begin a conversation like this.
"My parents told me when I was six.
I was found as a baby outside the hospital in Altona.
August 2007."
She looks at me for a long time.
"Which day?"
"Born on the fifteenth, found in the night of the sixteenth."
"Fifteenth of August," she says.
"It's in my file.
Abandoned, Altona.
I've been in the system since my first month."
The word system hits me harder than it should.
My mother sits on the board of two child protection foundations.
I know the annual reports, the graphs, the numbers.
I have never seen a person behind the numbers.
Now he is sitting across from me and has my face.
"There was nothing in my file about a sister," I say.
"A baby is easy to place."
Her voice is calm.
"Two are work.
So someone took one and left the other."
She doesn't have to say which of us was left behind.
"Tell me about yourself," I say.
She talks.
Not about everything; I can tell from the pauses.
Foster families in Harburg and Wilhelmsburg, a group home in Bergedorf.
For the past three years, a foster father in Steilshoop, Werner Koslowski, early retiree.
She says his name the way you give an address where you don't want to live.
"I'm good at maths," she says, almost apologetically.
"At everything with rules."
"Your presentation was good."
She laughs, short and hard.
"I stammered."
"Because you saw me.
I didn't take in a word from the others."
I lean forward.
"Your approach with the reductions.
I spent three months on that topic with a private tutor, and you made it clearer on a single slide."
"You had a private tutor.
For the application."
"For everything."
Now I'm the one apologising.
"Cello since I was four.
Mandarin, French, summer academy at Oxford.
My father wants me to go to ETH Zurich next year.
I wrote the MIT application in secret."
She raises an eyebrow, and for the first time I see the scar in it.
A fine pale line that parts the hair.
"Swing," she says when she notices my gaze.
"When I was seven.
The family back then thought the doctor was too expensive."
In return, I tell her about my peanut allergy.
About the satay skewer at a reception at my father's bank when I was eight, and the three days afterwards at the UKE.
Since then there has always been an EpiPen in my bag.
I show it to her as if it were proof that my life isn't made only of pearls either.
It isn't good proof.
We both know that.
"Sometimes," I say, "all of this feels like a cage.
Everything is planned.
The university, the degree, who I smile at at which ball."
"I would give a lot for your cage," says Cindy.
She doesn't mean it unkindly.
That is exactly why it lands.
And then I say it before I can think.
"Trade with me."
"What?"
"Not forever.
A week.
You sleep in my bed, I sleep in yours.
We look the same, Cindy.
No one would notice."
"You're crazy."
But she doesn't pull her hand away when I take it across the table.
"Let me think about it," she says finally.
We exchange numbers.
I type hers into my iPhone; she types mine into an old Nokia with a scratched display.
When we say goodbye outside the café, I hug her.
She goes completely stiff for a moment, then she puts her arms around me, carefully, like someone who hasn't done it often.
In the car to Blankenese, I look out at the Elbe and think that today I gained a sister.
What a trade like that might cost is something I don't think about.
Chapter 3
Cindy Bergmann
Hamburg, Hauptbahnhof, 28 August 2024, 10:00 a.m.
Six weeks.
Eight meetings, always in different cafés, never twice in the same neighbourhood.
Katharina has dictated her life to me like a vocabulary list.
Her mother is called Clarissa and calls her Käthchen.
Her father says things at breakfast like Excellence is not an act but a habit.
The housekeeper is called Frau Hansen and asks no questions.
Her best friend is called Sophie and talks so much that all you have to do is nod.
And cello lessons are cancelled this week because Professor Schneider is in Salzburg.
Katharina checked.
Twice.
I dictated my life to her.
It was a shorter list.
Two weeks ago we had a birthday.
Seventeen, both of us.
I celebrated it on a park bench in Planten un Blomen, with a piece of cake she had brought.
That morning her parents had given her a gold chain, with a pendant and her initials.
She showed it to me and said: "I'm going to wear this every day now.
Even with you.
So I don't forget who I am."
Now we're standing in the main concourse, next to the bakery, swapping.
She's wearing my jeans and my hoodie, her hair tied back in a careless ponytail.
Above her left eyebrow she's drawn a fine pale line with kohl and dusted it with powder.
From a metre away it looks like my scar.
I'm wearing her cashmere jumper, and my scar is hidden under her concealer.
I feel like I'm in costume.
We swap phones.
My Nokia for her iPhone.
We swap keys.
She keeps the chain.
"Werner is usually drunk in the evenings," I say for the tenth time.
"Drunk, he's predictable.
Stay in the box room.
Go to the school library during the day, it's open even in the holidays.
Frau Sommer is there."
"I'll manage."
"And if he gets weird…" I don't know how to finish the sentence.
I haven't told her everything.
Not about the nights I've heard his footsteps outside the door.
Not why the shelf in my room stands the way it does.
"If he gets weird, just leave.
Get out of the flat.
Call me."
"Cindy." She takes my hands.
"It's one week."
I should tell her.
Now, here, between the bakery and platform 14.
I should say: you don't know who he is when he's been drinking.
I don't say it.
Because part of me wants this week more than anything.
Seven nights in a room with a window.
Seven nights when I don't have to listen.
"One week," I say.
"One week."
She takes the U-Bahn to Barmbek and from there the bus to Steilshoop.
I get into the black car her father sent.
The driver nods at me in the rear-view mirror.
"Home again, Fräulein von Tiefenbach?"
"Yes," I say.
"Home."
Chapter 4
Katharina von Tiefenbach
Hamburg-Steilshoop, 28–31 August 2024
The lift is broken.
A note is stuck to it, the date on it is from March.
I climb eight floors.
The stairwell smells of cold smoke and something sweetish I don't want to know more about.
I stop outside the flat door, key in hand, and breathe as shallowly as I can.
Werner is sitting in the living room in front of the television.
A heavy man in stained jogging bottoms, his face grey with stubble.
Empty bottles stand in rows on the coffee table, as if he'd counted them.
"Where were you?"
"Out."
Cindy's voice.
Quiet, spoken downwards.
I've practised it.
"Make something to eat."
In the fridge there's beer and an opened salami.
In the cupboard I find canned ravioli.
I heat them up and bring him the plate.
He takes it without looking at me.
Then the box room.
Cindy described it to me.
Standing in it is something else.
Eight square metres, no window.
A mattress on the floor, a shelf of schoolbooks, a cloth bag with clothes.
The shelf isn't against the wall; it's positioned so you can shove it in front of the door with one push.
I only understand once I'm standing in front of it.
I sit down on the mattress and write to her.
I'm here. This is… hard.
The reply comes immediately.
Are you okay? Do you need anything?
Everything's fine. How about you?
Your bed is bigger than my room. Frau Hansen made me food. With vegetables. I don't know whether to laugh or cry.
Enjoy it.
The next morning I go to school.
The district school is a grey low-rise, the corridors empty, it's the holidays.
But the library is open, just as Cindy said.
A small room with worn books and a window onto the courtyard.
I take Cindy's maths exercise books from her compartment.
The margins are full of her small, precise handwriting.
Her solutions are shorter than mine.
More elegant.
My private tutor would have hated her, because she manages without him.
Around midday a woman appears in the doorway.
Mid-forties, tired eyes, a cardigan despite the heat.
"Cindy! Have you heard from the foundation yet?"
Frau Sommer.
"Not yet," I say.
"You'll do it."
She smiles with her whole face.
"You're the cleverest pupil I've taught in twenty years here. Don't let anyone tell you you don't belong there."
I can only nod.
This woman believes in my sister.
And my sister sleeps on a mattress behind a shelf.
In the evening Werner gives me no money.
I find the ten euros in Cindy's hiding place behind the baseboard and go to the kiosk.
Bread, cold cuts, milk.
Eleven euros twenty.
I put the milk back.
For the first time in my life I count the cost while shopping.
On the third evening Werner is different.
He calls me into the living room.
I'm to sit next to him, watch a quiz show with him.
He smells of grain schnapps and sweat.
"You've gone strange," he says.
"So quiet. So... refined."
"Just tired."
"Tired."
He laughs.
"From what?"
He eyes me from the side, too long.
"Seventeen now. Grown up."
I get up. "I'm going to bed."
His hand closes around my wrist.
"Did I say you could go?"
I tear myself free, run into the box room and shove the shelf in front of the door.
Now I know why it stands where it stands.
Outside, he curses.
Then his footsteps fade, the living-room door slams shut.
I sit in the dark, trembling.
I write to Cindy: Are you awake? I think I…
I delete it.
She's earned seven nights.
There are four left.
Everything's fine here. See you tomorrow.
On the fourth night, the night before 1 September, I wake because the shelf is moving.
Not much.
A few centimetres, a scraping across the floor.
Then again.
I feel for the Nokia and can't find it.
I feel for my bag and knock it over.
Something rolls across the floor, under the shelf.
In the gap of the door stands a shadow, broader than the hallway.
"Cindy," Werner says. His voice is completely calm.
"Now we're going to have a little talk."
Chapter 5
Cindy Bergmann
Hamburg-Blankenese / Steilshoop, 29 August – 2 September 2024
The bed is too soft.
I sink into it and still don't sleep.
The silence is too vast.
No television through the wall, no footsteps, only from far away the blast of a container ship on the Elbe.
In the morning I sit with Clarissa in the breakfast room.
A room just for breakfast.
Frau Hansen has baked croissants, there is freshly squeezed orange juice and three kinds of cheese.
I don't see this much food at Werner's in a month.
"You're so quiet, Käthchen."
"Just tired, Mama."
The word comes more easily than it should.
Clarissa smiles and strokes my arm, and I have to look down at my plate.
I learn quickly.
How to lay a napkin on your lap.
That Maximilian asks about school in the evening and doesn't listen.
That Frau Hansen sets a second croissant in front of me without saying anything, and that she looks at me as if she knows more than she says.
Katharina's messages come every evening, brief.
On 30 August she writes: All good here.
See you tomorrow.
On the 31st, nothing comes.
On the morning of 1 September I write to her.
Hey.
Everything okay?
The answer comes at midday.
all ok. need rest
I read it five times.
Katharina uses capital letters.
Katharina uses full stops, even in messages.
Katharina doesn't write need.
I call.
It rings until voicemail picks up, my own voice, recorded two years ago.
I call again.
The third time, the phone is off.
On Monday, 2 September, I wait until Clarissa has left for yoga and Maximilian is at the bank.
I don't take a taxi.
I take the S-Bahn and then the bus, like before, and only at the stop do I realise that Katharina would never take the bus.
Steilshoop looks different when you come from Blankenese.
Greyer.
The people at the stop are the same as always, but now I see them through her eyes, and I hate myself for it.
Eight floors.
The flat door is not locked.
"Katharina?"
No answer.
It smells of beer and smoke, as always.
And underneath, something sharp.
Chlorine.
No one in this flat has ever cleaned with chlorine.
The door to my little room is open.
The mattress is gone.
The floor has been wiped damp, in broad strokes that end at the door.
Only behind the shelf, where the mop didn't reach, there is still dust.
And in the dust, two parallel tracks, as if someone had dragged something heavy along the wall to the door.
I kneel down.
Something yellow lies under the shelf.
An EpiPen.
I hold it in my hand and cannot breathe.
She always had it on her.
Always.
She showed it to me like an ID card.
Werner is sitting in the living room.
The television is on, muted.
He turns his head slowly, and when he sees me, his face goes white.
"Where is she?" My voice is too loud.
"The girl who was here. Where is she?"
He stares at me as if I've come through the wall.
"You left," he says.
"You ran off."
"What did you do?"
"Nothing." His hands are shaking on his knees.
"There aren't two. There's only you. And you're gone."
I grab him by the shoulders.
He shoves me away, and I fall onto the carpet.
He stands over me, swaying, and for a moment I see something in his face worse than rage.
Fear.
Werner is afraid of me.
"Get out," he says.
"You don't live here anymore. You were never here."
I don't know how I get back.
At some point I'm sitting on Katharina's bed, the EpiPen in my hand, and outside it's growing dark.
I could go to the police.
I run through it, sentence by sentence.
A care-home kid from Steilshoop, living in a villa in Blankenese, claiming the daughter of the house is dead.
A drunk foster father who says he has no idea.
A wiped-down room.
No body.
And at the end of the sentence: me, Cindy Bergmann again.
Back in some room, any room.
I didn't tell her who he is.
I sent her there.
When Clarissa knocks on the door and asks if I'm coming to dinner, I wipe my face and say, "In a minute, Mama."
And as I walk down the stairs, the grief turns into something else.
Something cold and very calm.
Werner Koslowski will not sleep.
Never again.
Chapter 6
Cindy Bergmann
I learn Katharina the way one studies for an exam.
I read her diaries, her old school notebooks, her emails.
I watch the videos on her phone until I know how she laughs and how she tucks a strand of hair behind her ear when she's thinking.
Every morning I cover the scar in my eyebrow with her concealer.
The cello is the hardest part.
Professor Schneider returns from Salzburg in mid-September, and I tell him I sprained my hand on holiday.
That buys me two weeks.
I practise four hours a day, then five, until my fingertips split open.
Frau Hansen leaves plasters on my bedside table and says nothing.
Schneider hears me play for the first time in early October, eyes closed, his old hands folded in his lap.
"Different," he says afterwards.
"Technically weaker.
But there's something new.
As though you were working through something with the instrument."
"There's a lot on my mind."
He nods and doesn't ask further.
Sophie is more dangerous.
She turns up unannounced, throws herself onto my bed and talks.
About Mallorca.
About Charlotte.
About a Felix from a party in July.
"You were totally into him, Kathi."
"Oh, Felix," I say.
"That's over."
She studies me.
"You've really become strange."
In mid-September the email from the Lindqvist Foundation arrives.
Katharina von Tiefenbach has the scholarship.
Four years at MIT, beginning autumn 2025.
In my old inbox, which I open at night on her laptop, lies the rejection for number seventeen.
Politely worded.
They wished me all the best for my future path.
I sit for a long time in front of the two emails.
Then I reply to the foundation in my sister's name and accept.
Maximilian is angry at first, about the ETH, then proud.
Clarissa cries.
I smile into her embrace and taste ash.
At night I work on Werner.
In a mobile phone shop in Altona I buy a prepaid phone with cash.
On 12 September at three in the morning I send the first message.
I know what you did.
No answer.
But two days later I call at night, let it ring three times and hang up.
An hour later, again.
The week after, every night.
The spare key is still in the meter box in the hallway, where it has been for years.
One Thursday I wait until Werner leaves for the corner pub at nine.
Then I place Katharina's gold hair clip on his pillow.
It was in her jewelry dish; I've seen it a hundred times in the photos.
The next day I write: She sends her regards.
For the first time, a reply comes.
who are you
Your conscience.
One evening at the end of September I'm standing across from the pub in the shadow of a doorway when he comes out.
I don't pull the hood fully over my face.
He sees me, for a second, under the streetlamp.
Then I'm around the corner.
His Facebook password is the same as three years ago, when I set up the account for him.
At four in the morning, his page reads: I can't sleep anymore.
The dead won't leave me alone.
His pub friends comment.
You alright, Werner?
He deletes the post at midday.
He doesn't change the password.
In October I send him photos.
The Elbe at Wedel.
The Elbe at Övelgönne.
The Elbe at Blankenese in the morning fog.
Under each picture I put the same sentence.
The river gives everything back.
I don't know where she is.
I want him to believe that I do.
His posts become erratic, then they stop.
Frau Sommer writes to my old email address, asking if everything is all right, saying I haven't been at school since the holidays.
I don't reply.
Every word to her would be another lie, and I've had enough of those.
Sometimes, when I hold the prepaid phone in my hand at night, I wonder what Katharina would say about it.
I don't know.
I only knew her for six weeks.
On the morning of 4 November, Clarissa is sitting at the breakfast table with her tablet, reading the news aloud as she does every day.
"How awful," she says.
"They've pulled a dead woman out of the Elbe in Blankenese.
Right near here."
I set my cup down, very carefully, so it doesn't clatter.
The river gives everything back.
Chapter 7
Torben Mehring
Hamburg-Blankenese, Villa von Tiefenbach, 5 November 2024, 3:00 p.m.
The necklace cost me a whole morning.
Three jewellers on Neuer Wall; at the third, the saleswoman nods before I've even got the bag fully out of my pocket.
A custom-made item, engraving in English cursive script, collected on 14 August.
Ordered by Dr. Maximilian von Tiefenbach.
A gift for his daughter's seventeenth birthday.
I checked the system afterwards.
There is no missing person report for Katharina von Tiefenbach.
That is the sentence that sends me out to Blankenese.
The villa sits behind a beech hedge, a view of the Elbe, a gravel drive.
I park my Passat between a Porsche and a Mercedes and feel the way I always feel in places like this.
Like someone who is about to be asked for the tradesmen's entrance.
A housekeeper opens the door, mid-fifties, watchful eyes.
She leads me into a living room my entire flat would fit inside.
Oil paintings, a grand piano, and beyond the windows the Elbe, grey as lead.
Clarissa von Tiefenbach is slim, well groomed, friendly in the way people learn at boarding school.
I tell her we have recovered a piece of jewellery that may belong to her daughter.
I don't say where.
"Katharina is upstairs," she says.
"I'll fetch her."
I am left alone with the grand piano and the river.
On the mantelpiece stand framed photographs.
A girl with black hair at a cello recital.
The same girl in Paris, in Oxford, in a ballgown with pearls.
I step closer.
A beautiful, serious face.
Smooth, dark eyebrows.
Then she is standing in the doorway.
Seventeen, black hair, jeans and a pale cashmere jumper, barefoot.
The same face as in the photographs.
The same face as the one I saw last night on the forensic medicine table, insofar as the Elbe had left anything of it.
"Katharina von Tiefenbach?"
"Yes."
I take the bag from my jacket pocket and lay it on the glass table.
"Do you recognise this necklace?"
She doesn't go pale.
That strikes me.
Most people go pale, or red.
She goes still.
Her hand moves to her throat, where nothing hangs.
"That's mine.
I lost it."
"When?"
"In the summer.
Sometime in August, I think.
While I was jogging along the Elbe."
"But Käthchen," Clarissa says.
"You only got it for your birthday.
"You said you'd never take it off again."
"That's why I didn't say anything, Mama.
I was embarrassed."
A good answer.
Quick, and with exactly the right measure of embarrassment.
Too good for a seventeen-year-old, I think, and then I think that I am old and suspicious.
"Where did you find the necklace?" Clarissa asks.
"On the Elbe beach.
Yesterday morning."
As I say it, I look at the daughter.
"A young woman was wearing it.
We recovered her from the water."
Clarissa claps her hand over her mouth.
The daughter doesn't move.
Only her gaze drifts for half a breath to the window, to the Elbe.
"The dead woman was roughly your age," I say.
"Roughly your height.
And she was wearing your necklace.
I'd like to rule out any connection to you.
Would you consent to a saliva sample?
Purely routine."
Clarissa starts to say something, probably that she wants to call her husband first.
"Of course," the daughter says.
"If it helps."
I take the sample myself, two cotton swabs, inside of the cheek.
She opens her mouth without hesitation and looks at me as she does so.
Dark eyes, very calm.
I have seen murderers with calmer eyes, but not many.
On the way to the door she stops beneath the chandelier in the hall to shake my hand.
The light falls at an angle from above onto her face.
In her left eyebrow, beneath a layer of make-up, I see a fine pale line that parts the hair.
On the mantelpiece, in every single photograph, that eyebrow had been smooth.
I say nothing.
I thank her, walk down the steps and get into the car.
I sit there for a while, engine off, looking at the house.
On the first floor, a curtain moves.
Chapter 8
Torben Mehring
Hamburg, LKA / Steilshoop, 6–7 November 2024
My office at the LKA is twelve square metres and has a window facing the car park.
On the desk stand three coffee cups in various stages of being forgotten.
One bears the words Best Dad in the World.
My daughter gave it to me back when she still called.
The forensic medicine report comes in on Wednesday afternoon, faster than usual.
I pushed for it.
Doctor Aydın phones me instead of just emailing.
She never does that.
"Torben, the saliva sample from Blankenese.
And the dead woman.
The DNA profile is identical.
Not similar.
Identical."
"Contamination?"
"Two labs, separate runs.
No."
She pauses.
"There is exactly one explanation where both women exist.
Identical twins."
I hang up and sit still for a while.
Adoption records are sealed.
It takes a family court order, two phone calls with a judge who wants to go home, and an entire Thursday morning.
Then the file is in front of me.
Female infants, two, of Asian descent.
Found 16.08.2007, 03:20, outside the emergency room of Asklepios Klinik Altona.
Estimated age: approx. 24 hours.
Identical twins.
Child A: adopted by Dr. Maximilian and Clarissa von Tiefenbach, December 2007.
Child B: placed with a foster family.
First name assigned by case processing: Cindy.
Surname: Bergmann.
One child was chosen.
The other got her name from a case worker.
I enter Cindy Bergmann into the system.
One hit.
A missing person notification, filed on 15 October by the Wandsbek youth welfare office.
Cindy Bergmann, 17, has not attended school since the end of the summer holidays.
Foster father Werner Koslowski, Steilshoop, states the girl "ran off" in early September.
No report filed by the foster father.
A foster father whose child disappears, and who tells no one for six weeks.
I leaf through the youth welfare file.
Foster families, care homes, reports that all sound the same.
And right at the front, in an intake form from 2014, a handwritten note:
Old, poorly healed scar above the left eyebrow.
According to the child, a fall from a swing.
No medical treatment documented.
I call Aydın again.
"The dead woman," I say.
"Does she have a scar in her left eyebrow?"
She makes me wait while she goes through the photos.
"No.
The eyebrows are intact.
Why?"
Because the girl who shook my hand in Blankenese has one.
Because the girl in the Elbe is Katharina von Tiefenbach.
And because Katharina's parents have been having breakfast with a stranger for two months without knowing it.
Werner Koslowski lives on the eighth floor.
The lift is broken.
He opens the door a crack, the chain on.
A large, heavy man who has lost too much weight in recent weeks.
The skin hangs grey on his face.
He smells of grain alcohol and something older, sour.
"Criminal police.
Mehring.
It's about your foster daughter."
He stares at me.
His eyes are red-rimmed, the pupils too large.
"She's gone."
"We recovered a young woman from the Elbe, Mr Koslowski.
She looks like Cindy."
I had expected denial.
Anger, a lawyer.
Instead he unhooks the chain, opens the door and walks into the living room as though he's been waiting for me for weeks.
On the coffee table, among the bottles, lies a gold hair clip.
Next to it, a phone with a cracked screen.
"She comes every night," he says.
He sits down, hands between his knees.
"She calls.
She texts.
I saw her by the pub.
She put that on my pillow."
He points at the clip without looking at it.
"I got rid of her, didn't I... I got rid of her.
And she still comes."
"Who did you get rid of, Mr Koslowski?"
He doesn't answer.
He slides the phone across the table to me.
I scroll.
Dozens of messages from an unknown number.
I know what you did.
She sends her regards.
Photos of the Elbe, one after another.
The river gives everything back.
"She was different that night," Werner says.
His voice has gone very quiet.
"Cindy never screamed.
This one screamed.
She fought back.
I just wanted her to be quiet."
I take my dictation device from my bag and place it on the table, next to the hair clip.
"Werner Koslowski, I am placing you under provisional arrest on suspicion of murder.
You have the right to remain silent."
He does not remain silent.
He talks for an hour, in the living room, and then for another two hours at the station.
About the night of 1 September.
About the mattress he carried into his old Opel.
About the weight plates from the cellar and the clothesline.
About the Falkensteiner Ufer, where no one goes at night.
At the end he looks at me, and in his eyes there is something that almost looks like relief.
"The one who comes now," he says.
"It isn't her either, is it?
She's not Cindy either."
I don't answer him.
He is right and wrong at the same time, and I don't know how I would explain that to him.
Chapter 9
Torben Mehring
Hamburg, Police Headquarters, Interrogation Room 3, 8 November 2024, 10:00 a.m.
Interrogation Room 3 has no window.
A table, bolted down, three chairs, a camera in the corner with a red light.
Fluorescent tubes that hum as if they had something to hide.
Clarissa von Tiefenbach is sitting outside in the corridor.
She wanted to come in.
I told her that wasn't possible, and I didn't tell her why.
Beside me sits Ms Okafor from the Wandsbek youth welfare office, because the seventeen-year-old opposite me is legally under official guardianship.
She just doesn't know it yet.
She is wearing a dark coat over her cashmere pullover.
Her hands are folded on the table.
Today she has no make-up over her eyebrow.
She knows why she is here.
I switch on the recording device.
Date, time, those present.
Then I place two things on the table.
The gold chain in an evidence bag.
And a photograph from the youth welfare file: a seven-year-old girl with a fringe and a fresh, red line through her left eyebrow.
"Werner Koslowski confessed yesterday," I say.
"He killed Katharina von Tiefenbach in his flat on the night of 1 September.
He thought she was his foster daughter."
She looks at the photograph.
For a long time.
"I have to ask you something now," I say.
"What is your name?"
The silence lasts so long that Ms Okafor crosses her legs on her chair.
"Cindy," she says then.
"Cindy Bergmann."
She talks.
Calmly at first, in complete sentences, as if she had rehearsed it.
Perhaps she has.
The selection process in July.
The café.
The six weeks in which they dictated their lives to each other.
The main station.
"One week," she says.
"We were going to swap back on 4 September.
At the main station, by the bakery."
Then the message without capital letters.
The wiped room.
The EpiPen.
She reaches into her coat pocket and places it on the table, next to the chain.
Yellow, with the label of a pharmacy in Blankenese.
"She always had it with her.
Always.
It was under the shelf."
I look at it.
I think of Brenner, who would have turned over every flat in Steilshoop if someone had called her in September.
"Why didn't you come to us?"
She laughs.
It is not a pleasant sound.
"With what?
With an EpiPen and a wet floor?
Me, a girl from Steilshoop living in a strange villa, saying the daughter of the house is dead?
You would have sent me back.
And he would have said I was making it up.
That's what he always used to say."
"Used to."
She looks at the tabletop.
"I didn't tell her what he does at night.
I said he was drunk and predictable.
I wanted that week."
Her voice breaks for the first time, only briefly.
"I sent her there.
He killed her, but I sent her there."
Ms Okafor hands her a tissue.
Cindy takes it and doesn't use it.
"The messages to Werner," I say.
"The calls.
The hair clip.
That was you."
"Yes."
"He's a wreck, Cindy.
"He hasn't slept in weeks."
"Good."
She raises her head.
Her eyes are dry.
"I didn't touch him.
I only told him what he had done.
Every night.
I wanted him not to be able to forget it."
"That's not your job."
"Whose, then?"
For the first time she raises her voice.
"Yours?
There was no report.
There was no body.
There was only me, and officially I didn't even exist anymore.
What was I supposed to do?"
I have no answer I want to give her.
So I give her none.
In the end she asks only one thing.
"Did she suffer long?"
I think of Aydın's report.
Of the broken hyoid bone.
"No," I say.
It is the first time in this interview that I lie.
In the corridor, Clarissa von Tiefenbach stands up as I come out.
She has been crying, but not anymore.
I tell her, as briefly as I can.
The discovery.
The DNA.
Steilshoop.
I wait for her to fall apart.
She does not fall apart.
She sits back down, very slowly, like a much older woman.
"I knew," she says.
"Not knew.
But at breakfast she suddenly ate everything.
Katharina never ate breakfast.
I was pleased.
For weeks I was pleased that my child was finally eating."
She looks at the closed door of Interview Room 3.
"May I go to her?"
I don't know which of the two daughters she means.
I don't think she knows either.
Chapter 10
Torben Mehring
Hamburg, November – December 2024
Werner Koslowski hangs himself on the night of 11 November in the remand prison at Holstenglacis.
A torn sheet, the window bars.
The night-shift officer finds him at half past four.
On the table in the cell lies a note with a single sentence in block capitals.
SHE SHOULD STOP.
He did not write which of the two he meant.
Prosecutor Richter has her office on the third floor at Gorch-Fock-Wall, and she leaves me sitting in the corridor for twenty minutes before calling me in.
She does that to everyone who wants something from her.
"Stalking," she says, counting off on her fingers.
"Trespassing.
Data espionage, the Facebook account.
And a scholarship offer accepted under a false name.
That's not a minor offense, Mehring, that's fraud."
"She's seventeen."
"That's what the Juvenile Court Act is for."
"She spent her whole life in a system that passed her around like a parcel.
The last man she ended up with raped and strangled her sister.
The youth welfare office rated him suitable for three years."
"And she worked on him until he hanged himself in his cell."
"She told him every night what he had done. Nothing more. Without her we'd have no lead, no perpetrator, no confession. Just a dead woman with no name in the Elbe."
Richter looks at me for a long time.
She is a good prosecutor, and good prosecutors don't like it when police officers start talking about justice.
"You want to let her walk."
"I want her to get a chance. One single chance. Her first."
We reach an agreement after two weeks and three more meetings.
Dismissal under Section 45 of the Juvenile Court Act, with conditions.
Therapy, at least a year.
Eighty community service hours.
And the scholarship offer, which is in Katharina's name, is to be returned.
No one has to order that last part.
Cindy wrote to the foundation on 12 November.
She sent me a copy, without comment.
Three paragraphs, not a word too many.
At the end it says: The scholarship belongs to my sister. I don't want it. I would like to apply again, under my own name, if you will let me.
The von Tiefenbachs apply to the family court to take Cindy in as a foster child.
Maximilian comes to headquarters in person, in a tailored suit, and asks if I would write a statement.
He looks ten years older than in the photos on the mantelpiece.
I write it the same evening.
At the beginning of December I drive out to Blankenese one last time.
It's snowing, the first snow of the year, wet flakes that melt as soon as they touch the gravel.
Fairy lights hang in the windows of the villa.
Cindy opens the door herself.
She's wearing an old hoodie and jeans, and the scar in her eyebrow is visible.
She has stopped covering it with makeup.
"Herr Mehring."
"I just wanted to tell you it's over. The proceedings have been dismissed."
She exhales. "Thank you."
"Don't thank me." I stay on the bottom step. "A man is dead, Cindy. Not a good man. But you helped make it happen. You'll carry that with you."
"I know." She pulls her sleeves over her hands. "I'm already carrying a whole lot around. One more won't make a difference."
"It does," I say. "It makes a difference. It's supposed to."
She looks at me and nods.
Slowly, as if she has understood for the first time that I'm not here to take something from her.
"Why did you do it?" she asks. "With the prosecutor."
I think about it.
Over thirty years of files in which children like her appear as case numbers and eventually as the dead.
"Because the law is good enough for most cases," I say. "And because yours isn't one of them."
I walk to the car.
When I turn around, Clarissa is standing behind her in the doorway, resting a hand on her shoulder.
Cindy doesn't flinch.
The Passat starts on the second try.
I drive down the Elbchaussee, and the snow melts on the windscreen before the wipers reach it.
Chapter 11
Cindy Bergmann
Hamburg, auditorium of the International Gymnasium, 15 December 2024, 7:00 p.m.
Her name is still in the programme.
It was printed in October.
Katharina von Tiefenbach, violoncello.
Franz Schubert, Sonata in A minor D 821, "Arpeggione", 1st movement: Allegro moderato.
The headmistress asked whether she should cut the item.
Professor Schneider asked whether I really want to put myself through this.
Clarissa didn't ask anything.
The evening before the decision, she just stood in the doorway of my room while I was practising, and she stayed there until I was finished.
I stand in front of the mirror in the dressing room.
No concealer.
The scar looks like what it is: an old accident nobody ever took care of.
Maximilian knocks.
He is wearing a dinner jacket and holding his bow tie in his hand, because he hasn't been able to tie it himself in twenty years.
I tie it for him.
Katharina showed me how, in the café, with a napkin.
He watches my hands while I do it and says nothing.
Then he clears his throat.
"Excellence is not an act," he says, and his voice is not as steady as he would like it to be.
"Oh, forget it.
Just play."
The auditorium is full.
Parents in coats, teachers, pupils holding phones in their hands and then putting them away after all.
The story was in the Abendblatt, without names, but everyone here knows who was meant.
Sophie sits in the front row, her eyes already red.
Next to her, Clarissa and Maximilian.
At the edge of the third row, in her cardigan, Frau Sommer.
I sent her a ticket.
She came by bus.
The headmistress steps up to the microphone.
"The next piece was intended for Katharina von Tiefenbach," she says.
"Her sister is playing it.
Cindy Bergmann."
For the first time, my name stands before everyone in the room in this life.
I sit down.
The cello between my knees, the endpin in the wooden floor.
I think of the video on her phone, the one I watched three hundred times.
Her hands on that neck, calm and precise.
I play.
It is not her playing.
I stumble in the development, the semiquavers in the recapitulation are too fast because I am afraid of them.
But the theme at the beginning, that long, sad line that winds upward and falls back again, I play that the way I feel it.
Not beautiful.
True.
When the last note fades, there is silence.
For so long that I think I have done something wrong.
Then Frau Sommer stands up.
First.
And then everyone else.
Late that night, at home, I stand in front of the mirror in Katharina's room.
It is called my room now.
Clarissa says it as if she, too, has to learn it first.
On the dresser lies the gold chain.
Mehring sent it to me after the proceedings were dismissed, in a padded envelope, with a note: Belongs with the family.
I don't put it on.
I lay it in the drawer, with the EpiPen and the videos and the six weeks we had.
"I played your piece," I say to the face in the mirror.
"Not well.
But I played it."
The mirror doesn't answer.
It never has.
But for the first time, I don't see her in it.
I see a girl with a scar in her eyebrow who will take the bus to school in Steilshoop tomorrow morning because she wants to do her university entrance qualification there.
With Frau Sommer.
Under her own name.
Epilogue
Torben Mehring
Hamburg, LKA, 20 June 2025, 4:00 p.m.
Summer has finally arrived in Hamburg.
The sun throws bright rectangles onto my desk, and from the park across the street comes the smell of cut grass.
I close the last file of the day.
Homicide of Katharina von Tiefenbach. Suspect: Werner Koslowski (deceased). Proceedings dismissed.
Next to the file lies a card.
No heavy handmade paper, no gold edging.
A simple folded card from the copy shop.
Graduation ceremony, district school Steilshoop. 25 June 2025, 5:00 p.m., assembly hall.
Beneath it, in small, precise handwriting: You don't have to come. But I wanted you to know. The foundation interviewed me again in March. This time I didn't stammer. MIT, autumn. — C.
And below that, smaller, as though she had hesitated: Clarissa says you drink too much coffee.
I read the card twice.
Then I stand it upright against the mug that says World's Best Dad, where I can see it.
Cindy visits her sister.
The cemetery gardener in Blankenese, whom I once asked about something else, told me without my having asked.
Every Sunday.
Sometimes a woman comes with her, well dressed, waiting at the gate.
Sometimes both of them together at the grave.
I still don't know whether I did everything right.
A man is dead who should have stood trial.
A girl helped him die, and I made sure she barely paid for it.
There are colleagues who see it differently.
Richter sees it differently.
On some evenings I see it differently too.
But for thirty years I've closed files in which girls like Cindy Bergmann appear only once: on the last page.
This file is different.
In this file, her story goes on.
My phone rings.
Brenner.
"Torben. Harburg, a flat in the Phoenix quarter. Female, mid-twenties. Doesn't look like an accident."
"Address?"
I write it in my notebook.
The old one filled up in the spring.
The new one is still stiff and smells of leather, and the first page was empty until just now.
I take my jacket from the hook.
Before I turn out the light, I look at the card once more.
Twenty-fifth of June.
Five p.m.
Maybe I'll go after all.
I'd stand at the back, against the wall, where people are less likely to look at you.
Then I pull the door shut behind me and drive to Harburg.
